The first document, P 5232, it was signed by Mr. Stojic, and then we have another document a few days later signed by General Praljak. In the latter, we notice that the municipalities of Capljina, Citluk, Ljubuski -- and Ljubuski are mentioned, but in General Praljak's document we don't find Prozor, whilst in Stojic's document we had Prozor. The question arising here and that the Judges have to ask themselves, unlike what Ms. Alaburic may think, we need to know who does what. In your view, was it Mr. Praljak who had to take orders, as is seen here, or was it Mr. Stojic, in his position of minister of defence? Who has to do what, precisely? Here we can see that Mr. Praljak is taking a military order. He's issuing a military order that is normally in the purview of a military commander, since we're talking about military orders. But when you look at it together with the order or request by Mr. Stojic, they seem to match or to converge. You were on the ground, you examined all these documents. So in your view, who does what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I noticed the term "Prozor" being mentioned. Maybe it is an erroneous interpretation. What is referred to here are the same places. Both Mr. Stojic and Mr. Praljak mention the same municipalities under threat. At that moment, they were under threat, but they were not lost or had not fallen. In the order of Mr. Stojic, he regulates - and in my opinion, the first paragraph is the most important - defining all the structures who carry weapons, including hunting weapons, who are outside the structure of the armed forces, are hereby placed at the disposal of the military, and that order is to be carried out by the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO through his order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not want to testify, but in the case of witness -- the Bench was familiarised with the event which preceded these events discussed in this document, we just have to recall those events. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard what General Praljak said, Witness. There were events before the 20th and the 22nd of September. Does General Praljak's order fit in with all these prior events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Praljak was pretty clear. Sefer Halilovic was tried for those events, but was acquitted. You know about the massacres of Croatian population in the valley of Neretva, so this may be construed as a swift, desperate man's attempt to react to the situation. The fact that you are trying to mobilise hunting associations, this reflects that it is the 11th hour, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, Mr. Bos -- sorry. So, Witness, you cannot answer the question I put, who does what; was it within the purview of Mr. Stojic or that of General Praljak? You don't have an answer there. When you said that, I mean, it's the 11th hour, if you get down to the situation when you ask hunters to take their hunting rifles, the situation is of the utmost gravity, but who does what then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion is that by his document, Mr. Stojic has the right to mobilise or call up all armed forces which are wider than the armed forces proper, and subsequently Mr. Praljak, through his order, elaborates and gives effect to this order of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to move to Exhibit P 05799. Now, these documents, while you're looking at it -- this document is a document dated the 11th of October, 1993, and they are minutes of an extraordinary session of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, regarding the military and security situation on their territory. This document was also shown to you in-chief last week. Now, what I would like to point out is actually the second paragraph of these minutes which reads: "The officers of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna Armed Forces who attended this session, namely, Defence Minister Stojic, General Praljak, and General Petkovic, presented a report on the military and security situation on the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." Sir, first of all, does it surprise you that Mr. Stojic here is being referred to as an officer of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be an officer in the armed forces, you have to have establishment and rank. I know that Mr. Stojic is now a general, but he received that rank years afterwards. I do see this as an error of the minute-taker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. But isn't it correct, sir, and that's my second point, that in fact throughout the period that we've been going through, October 1992 all the way up to November 1993, Mr. Bruno Stojic regularly reported on the military situation to the government, first of the Croatian Community and that of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Mr. Bos regularly submitted. Well, if so, then the witness should be shown the regularity of those submissions. This is speculation, which should not stand at the beginning of their question. Mr. Bos should say, "On this session," "On that session," "On that other session, these things were proposed." And the witness has seen the records of all those submissions, and he can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, when you said Mr. Stojic regularly reported on the situation to the government, indicate the document, the date, and so on. Because if not, we get the impression that it was something that was customary; in other words, it was usual for this sort of meeting to be held. I mean, perhaps you're right in what you're doing, but we need to know the date. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If the witness could see the original of the document, I do believe that there is an error in translation. It says "Officials," "duznovnici," [phoen] and in the translation we'd have "officers." So could we take a look at the original document, please, at the second paragraph? At the present were officials, "duznovnici," not "officers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the original it says "duznovnici," which is "officials." I can't recall what Mr. Bos said initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, the English translation in fact reads officers rather than officials, so that means that in fact there is an error in the translation, which I regret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would seem it's a translation error, then, and it should say "officials" and not "officers." But, Mr. Bos, you said that Mr. Stojic regularly reported on the situation. Do you have dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me ask first the witness, and I have a couple of minutes, but I would first ask the witness, didn't he, himself, mention in the report that actually Mr. Stojic did report to the government .

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you mention that, yourself, in your report, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did. This can be easily verified. Mr. Stojic did submit reports. Unfortunately, I never saw the transcripts. I don't know whether those sessions were recorded. But the minutes, after all, are summarised, but by nature of his duties, Mr. Stojic could provide a rough picture of the military security situation. And I think that the details with respect to the army itself were given by officers of the Main Staff who would also come to attend those meetings several times, so I'm not quite clear, Mr. Bos, what precisely you are interested in. You have here -- in the paragraph prior to this, there's a discussion on the functioning of the civilian authorities, and that effect on the armed forces, and then one may ask whether all three gentlemen, Mr. Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak, are going beyond their competencies. But at that point in time, that was a key issue for survival. So the normative documents were not strictly adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have all these documents right here in hand, but I can give an example, another example. Witness, could I ask you to look at 1D 02179. 1D 02179.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So this is a record of a meeting dated the 4th of November, 1993, and item 1 on the agenda is: "Discussion on the current situation in the Vares area," and the first line reads: "The defence minister, Mr. Bruno Stojic, briefed the meeting on the military and security situation in the Vares area." Sir, could this be an time when Mr. Stojic would be reporting on the military situation to the government?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is beyond doubt. That can be from the item. The entire item provides a rough picture, judging by these minutes. But I don't see what is disputed here because, after all, as the head of the Defence Department, he had to know what was going on on the ground, due to his own duties with respect to logistics, et cetera. So in my view, it wasn't a high-level professional discussion. He would show the units on the map that would be beyond his competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Marijan - we are now in November 1993 - I would like you to look at a video-recording, and this is in Exhibit P 04238. And, Your Honours, this video has been shown to the Court before, when we showed a compilation of videos relating to Mostar, and this is a part from a BBC documentary dated the 10th of May, 1993, of which I would like to show a one-minute segment. And we'll be showing it in Sanction, Your Honours. Mr. Marijan, it will be subtitled in your language so you can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: "Reporter: A quiet day in Mostar. A former Muslim sniper position on fire, sporadic machine-gun, and mortar exchanges. The cease-fire has still not taken hold. It is the end of a dreadful week. "The Croatian forces, led by Defence Minister Bruno Stojic, put their wounded in Mostar at 150. Muslim casualties are certainly much higher. The total dead in the city could be as high 500. There are at least 200 Croats missing further north, and this may be just the start of it. "Over a map of the pitched battles, the minister says his forces could clear their half of the city in five hours, and he charges the Muslim commander with not wanting a cease-fire. "Interpreter: He's buying time. But this is one very bloody, very heavy war, and nothing can come as a surprise."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, this does show Mr. Bruno Stojic acting in a direct military role, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did see Mr. Stojic visiting the wounded. In my view, this is also beyond doubt, and he's talking to journalists. This is the first time I see an actual map. Now, whether this is indicative of a military role, I don't know what to say. It can be interpreted in different ways, but at least the introductory part was simply visits of the wounded. It's a bit unusual for me to communicate with foreign journalists. This should have been done by the Sector for Morale, even though that sector hardly functioned at all, so he frequently took over that role that should have been theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Does it surprise you to see Mr. Bruno Stojic in a military uniform, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this did not surprise me. It is a sort of traditional -- people -- everyone was wearing them, even now. I remember the Presidency of the SFRY who didn't have ranks, so were wearing uniforms. It was funny to see them, but this -- at the time of war, it was more like a folk costume. More people were wearing uniforms than not. Even nowadays, some people wear them as working clothes. So I don't think this is unusual. I saw Mr. Susak often in a uniform. I think Mr. Izetbegovic walked around in a uniform. True enough, he was the Supreme Commander, but this is not unusual. I don't think he had any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, after having seen this video and after having reviewed all the exhibits that we looked at in the last hour, and also after having reviewed the exhibits that were shown to you by Ms. Alaburic last week, is it still your firm position that Bruno Stojic, as head of the Defence Department, was nothing more than a civilian whose position in the HVO was purely administrative, as you said, and that he had no role at all in the command and control of the HVO forces? Are you still firm on that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am still firm in that position, but I would just like to add: Mr. Bos, we have seen your evidence, we have reviewed it. In the case of Ms. Alaburic, it was really running through the documents without any comments. So assuming that Mr. Stojic was in command, there should have been many more documents. He did have the right to communicate with the forces, but he used -- didn't use the proper terminology. That's also a linguistic issue, whether "order" and "commands" are the same thing. Most of the documents by Mr. Stojic that we have seen would not have lost anything in their value if he had written, instead of an "order," the word "request." So I think this also shows that he was outside the structures. I hope that Mr. Stojic will not hold it against me, but I think the rules of conduct and the rules of communication were violated by him, to a certain extent, the headings given to documents. But if you look at the contents, I don't think it is in question at all. He was expected to contribute to the combat readiness of the army, and I still stand by my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the one-minute video goes for a number of events; first of all, sniper shots. We can see on a building there are flames. We don't know where these shots are coming from. After that, we see Mr. Stojic, who was much younger at the time, wearing military garb. He goes to the hospital, where there are people who are wounded, but apparently the wounded people are Croats. So one might think that the sniper fire is Muslim sniper fire that's injuring Croats. We don't really know. But what is much more interesting is what comes later. Mr. Stojic is in his office. It's a very small office. It looks like a small secretary's office. It's quite tiny. There are two small tables, where the press -- perhaps international press members are there. There are a couple of young women in front of him, and he explains the situation. There are two things that I note. On the walls, we don't see any maps. There's virtually nothing on the walls. And we don't see any means of communication with what's happening in the field, if, in fact, he was the one who was in charge of operations from the office, but he's holding a document, a small document. It would seem that this is the position of certain forces. We don't know whether it's Muslims or Croats, and it's in blue and red. So it is a document of military origin, doubtless, which gives the position of forces. Is it a document that he has been given for the purposes of the press conference? There are a number of questions we might ask. Anyhow, you were in the field, and you went, I'm sure, to commanders' offices. Do you think, according to what we see in the video, Mr. Stojic is the chief of the army, or in his capacity as minister of defence, does he have full authority over everybody? What is the impression that you get from this video film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- I must admit, Your Honour, that you have a remarkable ability to notice things, some of which I myself haven't noticed, but you have. I would repeat what I've said. It is a bit unusual, let me use that term. You don't show the journalists military maps. This is simply, obviously, a sketch. Unlike that, there were large maps of Mostar with all the buildings indicated, and then there would necessarily have been a large map with every single building indicated, but we see Mr. Stojic with some kind of a sketch and he was doing what the head of the Department for Information should be doing, the person in charge of communication with the media. So from this, I cannot draw any conclusions that he had some responsibilities over the army, except that he was familiar with the situation on the front-line. But this is Mostar, and that is where his headquarters were. I don't know whether you've ever visited Mostar. It's not such a big town, and everyone knew everything, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document we see in Mr. Stojic's hands, it's a sort of sketch, giving the positions, but it's not a military map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was really something done in great haste, a rough sketch for the journalists who had come to the press conference, because a military map, after all, is something that the Main Staff has with all the forces indicated, and at least the brigades I have visited, these maps would cover entire walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, have you been to the office of the -- have you -- were you in his office, did you go to his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war, I did go to the office of the commander of the brigade and the Main Staff, too, in 1994-1995, when the HVO was at Kupres together with the ABiH, but this is something the journalists could not see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a brigade commander's office, what would you be struck by? What is there that shows that you're in the office of a military chief, what do you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first thing, in my view, the room of the commander of my brigade, it was a guards brigade, was quite large, and the first thing you see, at least what I noticed, were the flags of Herceg-Bosna and the banners of the brigade, then the coat of arms of Croatia and several maps that were on the walls. This was a period of peacetime at the time, so there would be a sketch of the brigade, but we went -- if we went into the field, we used a room for the operations centre, and the detailed situation on the ground would be indicated; that is, how we were deployed as well as the neighbouring units, so where they were deployed, on a broader area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Unless there are other questions, I'd like to move to another topic now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, so leave the binder aside for the moment. I'd like to move now to the topic of the -- of the military detention camps. Isn't it correct, Mr. Marijan, that the responsibility of the HVO -- Defence Department for the HVO military detention camps is limited to four paragraphs in your report, and in fact it's paragraph 70 and 71 which deal with the conditions of detention of prison camps, and paragraphs 119 and 120 of your report dealing with the establishment of Heliodrom? Isn't it true that those are the only four reports -- paragraphs in your report about the military detention camps?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is so, Your Honours. I refer to Heliodrom, as it is the only detention camp for which I found the decision by Mr. Stojic establishing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that the HVO Defence Department held de jure responsibility for the treatment of prisoners of war and military prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Your Honour. I object to this question. Mr. Bos needs to lay the ground for this question. After the expert report, which explicitly says what the responsibility of the Defence Department was in paragraphs 119 and 120, this question stems from nothing that Mr. Bos has said so far or that has been written in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm asking this question because Mr. Marijan, himself, last week, when he was being cross-examined by Ms. Alaburic, actually agreed to this, and I'll read out that part of the transcript. It's on page 49 of the 21 January transcripts, where the question is: "I have to repeat my question. You mentioned employee relationships. My question is: Under that term, do you imply the authority of the head of the Defence Department over prisoners of war, military prisons, military detention centres? Just give me a yes-or-no answer. We don't have much time to get into explanations. Just yes or no, please." And your answer is: "Yes, that should be the closest." But, sir, so -- but in -- anyway, let's -- we will also look and lay the foundation, and I'll ask you -- we'll go step by step, and I'll ask you first to look at Exhibit P 00292. Sir, I take it you have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Prosecutor, I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it says here, under Article 2: "The head of the Justice and Administration Department, in cooperation with the head of the Defence Department and the head of the Department of Interior, shall designate the locations where prisoners shall be kept, in accordance with the provisions of the aforementioned Convention in Article 1 of this Decree." And then Article 3, which is the one I would like to put emphasis on: "The Defence Department shall be in charge of the facilities stipulated in Article 2 of the decree." Sir, isn't it correct that on the basis of this Article 3, Mr. Bruno Stojic established the Central Military Prison of Heliodrom on 3rd of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is correct, but the interpretation I heard was "in December." Well, in effect, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: September, 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the decree was signed on the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at that decree, which is Exhibit P 00452. Is this, in fact, a decision in which Mr. Bruno Stojic established the Central Military Prison of Heliodrom and where, he, in fact, makes references to Article 2 of the decree that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I did write something about that in my report. There are certain differences from Article 2, because ultimately the explanation does not fit in with the preamble, because it transpires that the district and military prisons in Mostar were separated, and in the process the Interior -- Department for the Interior did not take part in this procedure, because -- the purview of those, of the Ministry of the -- Department of Justice and the Interior and Defence, but there's no doubt as to whether Mr. Stojic did establish this military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know whether any other military prisons were established in Herceg-Bosna in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a central military prison, in 1992, if I understood the question correctly, was the only such. They later on changed the label or the name, particularly during the conflict with the Army of BiH and during the Croatian-Muslim conflicts. There were several other such prisons cropping up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Right. Have you come across the names of prisons like Ljubuski, Dretelj, Gabela; have those names -- have you seen them before in documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisons were not of my particular interest, but I did see documents making reference to those prisons or having a connection with those prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, sir, is it correct that Mr. Bruno Stojic held responsibility military -- for those military prisons in the same way as he held responsibility for Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not easy for me to answer this question. I note that he established this one, and I believe that each prison has its unfortunately own not very illustrious story. I believe that we should take each of those prisons separately, and I believe that Mr. Prosecutor will come to that very soon, step by step, in terms of who is providing guards duty, the treatment of inmates, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you to look at Exhibit P 02679. Sir, this is a decision from Mr. Jadranko Prlic, dated the 8th of June, 1993, in which it's decided to set up a county military prison, and a county prison being settle up in Gabela. Now, have you seen this document before, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, sir, would it be correct that if an order here is issued by the president of the HVO government, setting up a county military prison, that Mr. Bruno Stojic, as a member of the government, would then become responsible for this prison?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. If I may, well, such worded question is very difficult to grasp. One establishes and the other person makes somebody else responsible. Why not Department for Justice or Department for Care for Refugees? I do believe that my learned colleague is overstepping the bordering of the cross-examination. If somebody else is establishing, how can Mr. Bruno Stojic be responsible for it? We should be laying foundations for connections with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another problem of process nature. We have an expert witness, not a fact witness. He produced his expert report in which he mentions one prison in four paragraphs. One concerns healthcare in prisons, the Department for Health is involved there, and the other three deal with the Heliodrom establishment. We came through the witness testimony to the organisation of prisons, we made mention of the guards and the internal structure of those prisons. What I believe the Prosecution must do is to lay the grounds. He should not be fishing for the name of a prison, Gabela, Dretelj, in the documents. We should hear whether the expert witness dealt with the prisons in preparing his expert report. The cross-examination went outside the boundaries of examination-in-chief. We were not given an opportunity to cross-examine on that. We should put an end to it. Let us hear whether the expert witness analysed this and whether he was examined in examination-in-chief about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I could just respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do respond, and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, if I can just point out where it says "the county military prison," I just established the foundation that Mr. Bruno Stojic was responsible for military prisons, and here we have Mr. Jadranko Prlic setting up a county military prison. So it seems to me a very logical conclusion to then draw that Mr. Bruno Stojic would be responsible for this military prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A very small and short question to relieve Mr. Karnavas. You're always speaking of a decision of Mr. Prlic. You're sure it's not a decision of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, as president of the HVO government, and I think I did point that out. It says here: "President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Jadranko Prlic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And it says that "at a meeting, the Croatian Defence Council reached the following decision." So I put it to you, this is a decision of the HVO, not of Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not disputing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We are going to have a 20-minute break. I think you have one hour and two minutes left, Mr. Bos. The Judges will endeavour not to ask questions so that we can finish the hearing normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, isn't it correct that the HVO Military Police Administration was given a role in the day-to-day operations of the military prison of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Military Police Administration provided security for the military prison of Heliodrom. I think there was a stamp -- a numbered stamp. Interestingly, they never put in the letterhead "The Military Police Administration" on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P 00514. P 00514. These are instructions from the chief of the military police, Mr. Valentin Coric, for the operation of the Central Military Prison of the HVO in Mostar. It's dated September 1992. Have you seen this document, and does it confirm that, in fact, the military police was responsible for the operation of the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen this instruction, and it confirms that the military police was in charge of providing security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether the military police was also in charge of security for similar camps like Ljubuski, Dretelj, and Gabela? Have you seen documents relating to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the topic of my analysis was the Defence Department, so I did not deal with prisons, in particular. I should see document by document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's just look at two exhibits which are --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. We've come to the crux of the matter, whether the -- the witness is now being -- asked to provide new expertise. If he is doing so, which was not the topic of the expert report that we received, then Mr. Coric's Defence demands cross-examination on that new expertise, because now the Prosecutor is soliciting new expertise. He's soliciting opinions on documents which were not the subject matter of his report, and we do not have time for cross-examination. Recently, the witness said that he did not deal with prisons, and I had no opportunity to cross-examine the witness because that was not the subject matter of his expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please stick to the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll ask you then, Mr. Marijan, could you go to your expert report, and I'll ask you to look at paragraph 120 of your report. And I'm going to read out the sentence that I'm, in particular, interested in, which reads as follows: "On 14 August 1993, Stanko Bozic, director of the Central Military Remand Prison, whom Stojic had not appointed to that position, requested that had Stojic used his authority to ensure food for 2.100 prisoners in the Central Military Remand Prison." And there's a reference here to Exhibit P 04186. And, Mr. Marijan, I'm curious why you --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I apologise. I would ask the learned friend to either read the subsequent sentence before answering or for Mr. Bos to read the subsequent sentence, because sentences without their context could mislead us in our conclusions, and the following sentence explains the crux of the expert opinion of this expert witness, and it explains the circumstances leading to the detainees being in that detention prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, everyone here in the courtroom has read this report, and I really don't see the need to add, you know, additional text for the context. I mean, I take it that everyone has read the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, we have seen and read this report, but the next sentence explains that the persons, the subject of the question of Mr. Bos, are housed outside the facility which Mr. Stojic established. So Mr. Bos should first ask where they were housed, pursuant to whose decision, and how the accommodation of those persons in those facilities, which were not established pursuant to Mr. Stojic's decision describing the Central Military Prison, and who could be responsible for those. For that reason and not for the purpose of interfering with my learned friends, the sentence I'm referring to refers to persons outside the Central Military Prison facilities and explains who took the decision for that to be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, what I'm interested in is the sentence where you say: " ... whom the head Stojic had not appointed to that position." And you're referring to Mr. Stanko Bozic and you're claiming that Mr. Stojic hadn't appointed that position. Now, let me ask you, why did you mention that in your report, that Mr. Stojic hadn't appointed this decision? What was the purpose of that? It seems to imply that by mentioning this sentence, that Mr. Stojic didn't have any responsibility over Mr. Bozic. Is that you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, by this sentence, I wanted to say exactly that. Pursuant to the 3rd of September decision, apart from the decision on establishing the prison, there is also a regulation or provision on the appointment. I -- to the best of my knowledge, that person was not that appointed person. I never saw a decision appointing Mr. Bozic by Mr. Stojic to be -- to head that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who actually appointed Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall seeing a document appointing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to move to Exhibit P 00352. Now, sir, this document is a diary from Mr. Josip Praljak, and I think you have been referring to this document as well in your reports. Is it correct that you have seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I read parts of this journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to go to page number 20 of the English version. It's the entry of 20 December 1992. So on the entry of 20 December 1992, second column: "Working meeting with Chief Valentin Coric ..." And then I'll read out the second indent: "Chief Valentin thanked Mile Pusic for his work and introduced the new warden appointed by his written order." And at the end of that entry it says: "Mr. Stanko Bozic, the new warden, met everyone in the prison and said his arrival would change nothing in the prison, and, 'I would like to have good cooperation with everyone.'" 20 December 1992. Sir, would you agree with me, on the basis of what I just read out, that it was Mr. Valentin Coric who actually appointed Mr. Stanko Bozic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My learned friend misread. If we're reading the Croatian text - it's on the screen - it nowhere says that Mr. Coric appointed anybody. It was appointed by a written order, but it is not stated whom appointed whom. It is illegible, and it's in very poor shape. Also, Mr. Bos said that Mr. Coric called the meeting to order, but in the document, the document reads Warden Mile Pusic called the meeting to order. This is a private diary in longhand, and can we have the text read correctly? Maybe the witness can read it out in Croatian, the contentious paragraph, for everybody to see whether everything is in order. The document says: "Valentin thanked Mile Pusic ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe it would be good if the witness could read out this part of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, could you read out the part where it starts -- well, in English, it says, "Chief Valentin thanked Mile Pusic ..."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Chief Valentin thanked Mile Pusic for his work and introduced the new warden appointed by a written order ...," and I cannot read further. The text is unintelligible. There are two other words that I can't make it out. "He paid attention to the work ...," and then illegible: "... prison, particularly the work of policemen, shift commanders ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You can stop there. It -- it's -- what's important is that sentence where there, you know, where he says written order or -- but it doesn't say "his" but it's -- it appears from what you're reading out that it doesn't. Now, could I ask you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: There is not the translation. I'm sorry, Mr. Bos. The last sentence of what you have said, there was no translation and no English text was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think from what the witness read out, it remains unclear by whom the written order was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to be very careful at all times when it comes to translations. You have to keep a tight watch, because we work in three languages. So sometimes, you know, you hear something that is not right. I'm looking at the English translation. It says "his order," which leads one to believe that he was appointed by Mr. Coric. But as read by the witness off the B/C/S text, it is "a," "an" or "a written order," which is not necessarily issued by Mr. Coric. Yes, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to intervene concerning one word. If you take a better look at the Croatian version, somebody said "appointed," but the letter E can be made out, so this is "appointment," and not "appointed," which confirms your thesis that it is unknown who appointed. It was interpreted "appointed," as a verb, but in the Croatian you can make out the letter E and another letter which should spell "imenovanje," which is "appointment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to move, in the same document, to the 22nd of March, 1993 entry, which is on page 25 of the English version. And in order not to get confused again, maybe you can read out the entry starting on 22 March 1993, starting at -- with the line: "At 0930 hours ..." Could you please read that out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At 9.30, Stanko Bozic came to me, to the prison office. After a short conversation, Bozic told me that he had come back to work in the prison again, that it was a mistake to leave, and that he was with Chief Valentin Coric, who told me he can work in the prison again. "I immediately called the chief, Vale. He confirmed this orally and told me to let him do the job he used to do as warden and just to continue doing it as if he had not stopped. "I informed him about what had happened during his absence and took over responsibility for the prison and life in it. "I wrote a report on that arrival and take-over and sent it to the head, Bruno Stojic, and Chief Valentin Coric."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, doesn't this entry imply that, in fact, Valentin Coric appointed Mr. -- at least, you know, had authority over Mr. Stanko Bozic and that he, in fact, appointed him as warden of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a bit-confused passage. Some things are missing. I wouldn't dare clearly state that this was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, we see at the end that, also in your report, it was sent to Mr. Bruno Stojic about the arrival of Mr. Bozic. Would you agree that Mr. Valentin Coric did his work at the Detention Unit as a direct subordinate of Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I -- we have such confused translation or interpretation. Could my learned colleague repeat the question, because I could not make out the gist of his question in the interpretation that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If you look at the 22nd March entry at 1993, the last sentence, it says that: "I," and which is Mr. Josip Praljak, "wrote a report on his arrival and take-over and sent it to the head, Bruno Stojic, and Chief Valentin Coric." And then my subsequent question was: Sir, isn't it correct that Mr. Coric did his work at the detention unit as a direct subordinate of Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since there are two Praljaks, it is always necessary to specify Josip or Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we should split this question into two. I don't know how Mr. Bos concluded that Mr. Coric worked at the detention centre. It is completely unknown to me. And then ask under whom -- whose authority. This is completely unintelligible. We have sentences which are unintelligible in Croatian, let alone in English, and he's showing them to the witness out of context. We had a witness - he's not a protected witness - who testified here, who authored this document, and this should have been asked of him. Now we're trying to get to the bottom of this, what the poet wanted to say, and the poet is back in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he's not here, and we're now trying to analyse his opus with a man who has no knowledge of the facts of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, the question is who appointed Josip Praljak warden of the prison; was it Mr. Coric or somebody else? We're not going to spend the entire evening on this, so put the question to him, and the expert witness will give us his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, let's leave aside the appointment of Mr. Stanko Bozic, and I'll put my last question -- I'll ask my question in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We've established that Mr. Valentin Coric was responsible for the operation of the Heliodrom. We've established that with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know when we established that. The witness has said repeatedly that the military police was responsible for the security. I don't know who established this. We haven't yet established that here in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Bos, you're saying that it was established that he was responsible for the operation of the Heliodrom. What do you base your conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase it, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We've established that the military police was responsible for the security of the Heliodrom; would you agree with me on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Bos, the military police was in charge of the security of the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that Mr. Valentin Coric was head of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct, but the prison is not part of the structure of the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Prosecutor to make a distinction between the Heliodrom centre, with all its contents, and the Heliodrom prison. So when he's asking the witness a question, to state clearly who provided the security for the Heliodrom centre and who for the prison. These are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm talking here about the Heliodrom military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that for the security of the Heliodrom military prison, the military police, of whom Mr. Valentin Coric was the head, was responsible for the security of that military prison?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me, Mr. Marijan, that Mr. Valentin Coric was a direct subordinate of Mr. Bruno Stojic in the structure of the HVO Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was subordinate to Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another exhibit, which is P 00665. This is an order from Mr. Bruno Stojic, dated the 28th October 1992, and it orders that all prisoners of war held by the HVO be unconditionally released from HVO military investigation prisons. And I would like to focus your attention to the last sentence of that paragraph, which reads: "I hereby place Mr. Valentin Coric, head of the HVO Military Police Administration, in charge of carrying out this order." Sir, doesn't this show what we just established, that Mr. Bruno Stojic had authority over Mr. Valentin Coric when it comes to the security of the HVO Central Military Prison, and in fact it refers here to --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, which military prison? Which military prison, Your Honours? Which military prisons? On the 28th of October, 1992, Mr. Bos is making generalisations. This is a specific issue. Which prison existed at the time? He hasn't laid the foundations for this question as to which prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, it's a fact, it reads: "HVO military investigation prisons," so it's all investigation military prisons that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the text, one can make that conclusion. Further down, there's specific mention of Mostar, Livno and Tomislavgrad, so this was on the basis of an agreement. I think there's a series of documents regarding the release. This was agreed upon at the beginning of October. These were just prisoners of war. As far as I remember, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's leave this document aside and let's move back to your report, paragraph 120, which we had before. I would like to ask you a question about your reference to the 2.100 prisoners that were being -- to which you are referring to in your report. Sir, in your understanding, did -- these 2.100 prisoners that you referred to, were these people civilians, prisoners of war, or military prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question. I heard another number in the headphones, but you're probably referring to the number 2.100. There was some confusion. I heard a different number. I must admit that I didn't study prisons, and I really don't know whether these 2.100 were civilians, or soldiers, or a mixture of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it not true that these thousands of detainees were, by majority, Muslim men of military age who had been arbitrarily arrested by the HVO after the ABiH attack on the Northern Barracks on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a compound question, a number of questions are included. Perhaps it can be broken down and the foundation laid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that these 2.100 men were all Muslim men of military age?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at a document. Maybe that's easier. Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 03663. Sir, this is a report from Officer Zvonko Vidovic from the Crime Prevention Department of the military police, and it's reporting on a meeting in Ljubuski on the 22nd of July, 1993, and at this meeting Mr. Valentin Coric was also present, as we can read in the first paragraph. And I'd like -- I'll read out the third and fourth paragraph of this report, and then I'll ask you some questions: "Consequently, all those persons who have been detained, but against whom no criminal proceedings have not been initiated (or against whom a criminal report has not been filed) are, according to the order of the chief of the Military Police Administration, unknown to our department. This refers solely to the large number of Muslims who have been brought unselectively to the Central Military Remand Prison buildings and who have since been forgotten. By inertia, the Crime Prevention Department has conducted interviews with more than 2.000 people, and none of them were interesting from the standpoint of crime. Therefore, the question about the domain of our activities was justifiably put to the Military Police Administration Chief, Mr. Valentin Coric, who issued the above order for us to begin handling criminal cases. "As the head of the Department for Administration and Justice was charged with drawing up a report on the Central Military --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: " ... was charged with drawing up a report on the Central Military Remand Prison, it follows that according to the decisions of the institutions of this department, it's the duty of the Department of Justice to appoint the Central Military Prison warden and to make all decisions with regard to the detainees. As for disciplinary measures against HVO soldiers, they will be resolved by those who pronounce them, but we believe that among the 2.000 people who were unselectively brought to the premises of the Central Military Prison, there is a fair number of those who are of interest for security and who should be found and processed, which is precisely the job of the Information and Security Service." Sir, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure about this document, whether I've seen it before or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in the third paragraph, the Crime Prevention Department conducted interviews with more than 2.000 Muslim people arrested and detained at Heliodrom and concluded that none of them were interesting from the standpoint of crime?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the basis of this paragraph, one can make that conclusion, though here there's reference to 2.000 persons, but one can infer that they were Muslims and, as you have said, that none of them were interesting from the point of view of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it not correct, sir, that as a result, the Military Crime Prevention Department referred to the HVO Department of Justice to make decisions with regard to these 2.000 detainees and to the SIS for the possible security reasons? That's in the last paragraph of this document that I read out.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is their proposal, that they are suggesting that a representative of the Department for Justice deal with this problem with the prison, whereas a part of those 2.000 persons, who may be of interest for security reasons, that the Security Service should conduct interviews with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it not correct that, in fact, the HVO authorities didn't know what to do with these 2.000 Muslim men at Heliodrom, who, as it's stated here, were unselectively brought to the premises?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, all I can say, on the basis of this, is that 2.000 persons were unselectively brought there. It is not clear who brought them there. And I wouldn't say that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna didn't know what to do with them. This is not something we can infer on the basis of this text alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look, then, at another document, which is Exhibit P 06729. Sir, this is an SIS report dated the 18th of November, 1993, on the works of Gabela and Heliodrom, and the report starts on Gabela, and it says "Report number 1," and then the situation of the prisoners of war, and it reads as follows: "There are about 300 prisoners of war in each of the said facilities. There are currently 1.268 prisoners of war. All prisoners of war are persons of Muslim nationality, male, and there are some of them (I have not been able to establish the figure precisely) who are under 18 and some who are above 60 years ..." And it continues: "In the brief personal context with prisoners of war, the impression is that many of them have been brought to the shelter from their homes, street, or work-places, while the rest have been captured during the combat operations. Although there are no precise numbers for these categories, the fact is that so far nothing has been done to separate, provide accommodation, and apply all other criteria to these two so-called categories of persons housed on the premises of the shelter." And then if we then continue to the situation in Heliodrom, which is on page 5 of the English version of the document under item number 2, again the accommodation of prisoners of war, here it reads: "In the said facilities, there are 2.600 prisoners of war who are of the same category as the prisoners of war in the previous shelter, of the same category; that is, real prisoners of war have not been separated. Members of BH Army have not been separated from civilians who have been brought (for various reasons)." If we move to page number 6, in the English version it's under the item, "Command and Control in the Shelter and Security System," third paragraph: "His main problem at the moment is the chaotic way in which persons are brought to the shelter. According to him, people are brought on a random basis, according to some personal criteria, while any opposition to this may even result in threats with weapons to anyone who would disagree." Sir, doesn't this in fact show what I just read out to you, that these people had been randomly arrested?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can see from this that in these several camps, there was a large number of people who were unselectively arrested. There are obviously prisoners of war, but there are also persons, judging from the first part that you read out, that are some under 18 and some over 60 years of age. It isn't stated anywhere who brought them in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I'll try and make this my last intervention. The date is the 18th of November, 1993. Mr. Bozic tells us that -- says that the greatest problem is the unselective arrest. He's talking about that period of time, the 18th of November. Now, from the interpretation given, it says if they were brought in now, at that time. I wish to draw attention to the fact that Mr. Bruno Stojic at that time was not head of the Defence Department, so this is beyond the scope of what the expert has analysed in his report. This is a reference to unselective bringing in of prisoners at that point of time and not at any time, when Mr. Bozic was not -- when Mr. Bruno Stojic was not in charge of this department.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to disagree here with counsel. There's no way that the document reads that these people have been arrested on the 18th of November. I think it's clear from the document that there has been reference here to a problem that already existed even before the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, sir, we'll leave this aside, and I'll ask you to go back again to paragraph 120 of your report. Sir, you've been referring here to this letter from Mr. Stanko Bozic on the 14th of August, 1993, to Mr. Bruno Stojic, which is P 04186. I'm not asking you to go to that document, but isn't it true, sir, that there were at least four more letters from Bruno Stojic -- from various authorities, I should say, from the Heliodrom which were addressed to Bruno Stojic in 1993? Have you had -- is it correct that you have come across other reports that were addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have said several times I didn't go into this issue, in particular. I do know that I did see some reports. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at those reports, Mr. Marijan. Could I ask you to look at P 04352. This is a letter from Mr. Stanko Bozic addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic, dated the 20th of August, 1993, and it says: "I'm writing to inform you of the visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross to the Central Military Remand Prison and the objections they made to me." And then I'll move on a bit. It says: "Mr. Franco pointed to the following wrongdoings and violations of the Geneva Conventions: Sending detainees to work; to the quality and quantity of food, they request its improvement; and, 3, the bad conditions in solitary cells. Regarding the violations of the Geneva Conventions, Mr. Franco warned and obligated me, as a warden, to ensure that these wrongdoings are not repeated in the future, or we would be reported to the International Tribunal. "After the Red Cross departure, we were not able to remedy these wrongdoings. On the contrary, the number of wounded and killed at the workplace is increasing by the day." And then it concludes: "Please help us to resolve this problem in this new situation so we could protect the Central Military Remand Prison, the HVO Command, and the interests of our whole people." Sir, had you seen this letter before, Mr. Stanko Bozic's address to Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at another letter, which is a month later, the 29th of September, 1993. It's Exhibit P 05477. Sir, this is a letter from Mr. Zvonko Vidovic of the Military Crime Prevention Department, addressed to Mr. Stojic personally, in which -- well, I won't read out the whole letter, but it concerns the unapproved release of by Mr. Miladan Halitovic [phoen], Tuta, of four Croat murderers who are kept at the detention centre in Heliodrom; P 05477. I'm sorry, I'm moving a bit fast, but I'm also looking at the clock. So, sir, this is a letter from Zvonko Vidovic, head of the MP Crime Department, addressed to Mr. Stojic, and it concerns the unapproved release by Miladan Halitovic, Tuta, of four Croat murderers who were kept in detention at Heliodrom and who were released to fight in Rastani. Now, what I will read out is the last -- the one-but-last paragraph of this letter, which says: "To use your influence and position to resolve the Central Military Police -- to resolve the Heliodrom problem as soon as possible, because it's now more than obvious that the HVO disciplinarian measures are not followed, that people are brought and taken away without anyone being told. The hierarchy and orders of superior officers are not being followed, and it seems that anyone can order the release of certain detainees without consulting the police or judiciary, not to mention the situation with detainees of Muslim nationality." Sir, have you seen this letter addressed to Mr. Stojic before?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't kept my promise. In the original, there's references to the detainees, persons detained, and they were detainees. If they were HVO members, they were detained for the commission of crimes, so they were not prisoners. In the original, it says "detainees." Therefore, these questions and this document deals with the question of detainees; that is, members of the HVO detained for crimes, rather than prisoners, and that is what is stated in the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But the report is being addressed to Mr. Stojic, personally, isn't it, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the report is addressed to him, and it seems to have been received by the Defence Department. The previous document did not have this stamp, but this one does, the reception stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's move to the next exhibit, P 05812. Again, it's a letter addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic, this time from the warden of Heliodrom, Mr. Stanko Bozic, and he's -- in fact, and I'll summarise what's in the document. He's reporting a number of issues that are in relation to -- in relation to Heliodrom. There's, in fact, eight issues. And -- well, you can read for yourself what the problems are. Let me just read the last line of this letter, which says: "As I'm not able to solve these problems alone, I appeal to you to use your influence for these problems to be solved." Sir, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I mainly reviewed the documents received by Mr. Stojic with the reception stamp. It is possible that I did see this one, but I can't guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, finally, let me look at the letter dated the 26th of October, 1993, which is P 06170. Sir, this is a document from the deputy warden, Mr. Josip Praljak, and it's a report on the work of the Detainee Release Commission, and it starts off by saying: "By the order of President Bruno Stojic ...," and then it refers to a number of 6 August 1993, "... which entered into force on 10 August 1993, and a member of a commission to establish greater order in prisons, and of other authorities which were decreed because of the large number of detainees accommodated in three facilities; the prison building, and two other facilities which were not designed for use as prisons." Sir, this paragraph refers to an order by Stojic dated the 6th of August. Do you recall which order this is, the order establishing the Detainee Release Commission? Have you seen that order before?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe if we can just look at that document. It's P 03995. So this is an order by Mr. Bruno Stojic, ordering that as of the 10th of August, 1993, the commission authorised by the Department of Defence is to take charge of all Detention Unit and prisons in which prisoners of war and military detainees are held, "... and it will be composed of the following:" And then follows five names; number 1, Berislav Pusic, Josip Dokic, et cetera, and number 5, Josip Praljak, the one actually drafting that letter that we just looked at. Have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marijan, based on all these documents that we've been -- that I've been showing you, wouldn't you agree, isn't it correct that Mr. Bruno Stojic not only had de jure responsibility for the military detention centres, but that in effect he was also considered as the de facto superior responsible person, at least by those who were running the day-to-day operations in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, from these documents that have been shown to me, one can see that wardens wrote those reports addressed to Mr. Stojic. And regarding one or two of them, I'm quite sure that Mr. Stojic did receive them, because they bear the reception stamp. And that is all that I could say, in concrete terms. But as I have been saying, my interest in prisons was very minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that the Ministry of -- the Ministry or -- the Department of Defence also had responsibility for the conditions of the camp through its Sector of Health Services, which was led by Dr. Bagaric, and isn't is it correct that paragraphs 70 and 71 of your report deal with this particular responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what can be said with certainty is that the Health Sector did endeavour to improve conditions, and I came across only such documents. Now, whether this can be interpreted as their responsibility, I don't know, but that members of the Health Sector did draw attention to these responsibilities, that is beyond doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And isn't it true, Mr. Marijan, that in fact they drew up reports on the conditions of detentions not only for the Central Military Prison of Heliodrom but also for all other military detention facilities in the Herceg-Bosna region?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't state that with certainty. I do know that I saw some, but whether they related to all those institutions, I can't say. I simply can't confirm that I saw them relating to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at P 06858. This is a report from Dr. Ivo Curic, dated the 24th of November, 1993. And, sir, isn't it correct that this report on the conditions not only of Heliodrom but a number of prisoners that are -- of prisons that are -- locations that are mentioned in the first column of this chart -- in fact, it lists Heliodrom, Gabela, Ljubuski, Livno, Duvno, Prozor, and then it says "Rakitno" and "Drbkrovici" [phoen] - sorry, it's a bit late - who both don't exist anymore?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not see this document before, but it's not quite clear to me. I didn't know that Livno had this type of prison. But that it was signed by a person from the Health Sector, that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, I look at the clock and it's 7.00, and I think I have 15 more minutes left, and I think it would be better if I continued tomorrow those 15 minutes. One-five, 15, a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, indeed you have 15 minutes left. You're entitled to use them. It's your basic right. In other words, the witness will be forced to stay overnight. We have wasted a lot of time with objections, with the requests for disqualification. I can't wait to see it on my desk, if the Alaburic Defence maintains their opinion. So, Ms. Nozica, do you have any redirect? Given the time you've used, you don't have time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have some questions for the redirect. And according to my calculation of time, I think that time can be deducted from the total amount of time I have envisaged for my case. I will be doing my redirect even if I find myself in a situation of not being able to call my witness. I will simply fit into the time allotted to me for the presentation of the Defence case for Mr. Stojic. So I do have some redirect for this witness. And I wish to say that I'm aware that we are ready with our next witness. So immediately after the end of the 15 minutes and the redirect, we can proceed with the next witness, if the Trial Chamber is agreeable. So could you please give me instructions, because it is important for me to know whether I will be continuing with my next witness tomorrow. As for the redirect, I should need at least one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want one hour for redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, the Trial Chamber said that, in terms of evaluating the time, we include the time for examination-in-chief and redirect. This was always our rule. You have been given a lot of time already, and now you want one extra hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I'm afraid that I didn't get anything from the Trial Chamber. What you gave me for the examination-in-chief for this witness was deducted from my total time. My understanding of your decision is that I affix the time for the direct examination, and if I need more for the redirect, it is deducted from the total amount of time allotted to me for my Defence. I will not always have a redirect. This time, I will. So would you please deduct the time I use for redirect from my total amount of time? Because, Your Honours, it is very difficult to envisage, when you start with a direct, whether you will need time for the redirect. The redirect depends on the cross-examination, and I could not envisage, when I brought my witness, that I would need time for the redirect. So I would ask that I be allowed the time I need, and please deduct that time from my total time. If, in the future, we will be working differently, then I will need to know that. So sometimes at my expense, I will spend less time on the direct. I won't be able to ask all the questions I need, and I may not need any redirect. So I think redirect should be deducted from the total time for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Redirect is only authorised to the extent of the cross-examination, so when you cross-examine -- for instance, "The Prosecutor showed you a document, I have a question on that document," or, "I'll show another document," so we agree on the extent and scope of redirect. But as a rule, when you assess the time you need, you must take into account the time you might need for redirect, because with the system, each time you're going to take time out of your time credit, and at some point you won't have any left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may try to assist. Of course, in an ideal world, it would be no doubt advantageous if counsel could predict the future and could know, to a nicety, the questions that were going to be asked by the Prosecution and by the opposing -- the other parties in this courtroom. Of course, reality is not like that. And as my learned leader put it, until the Defence for Mr. Stojic, and it will apply to the other accused in due course, see the nature and scope of cross-examination, it is exceptionally difficult to predict the extent of the necessary re-examination arising out of the cross-examination that is being conducted by the other parties in this courtroom. Your Honour, in my respectful submission, a margin of deference must be given to counsel in this courtroom. That must apply to all parties, the Prosecution and the counsel for the different Defence teams, as to how they think it most appropriate to use the time that is being bestowed upon them by the Trial Chamber to fulfill their primary task of effectively and properly defending their clients. Your Honours, there's no possible prejudice, in my respectful submission, to this Court or to the parties if counsel in this case -- my lead counsel, wishes to deduct time from the quantum that is being given by the Trial Chamber, and nips and tucks are always possible in the course of a trial. And if there is a miscalculation, well, that must be on the head of the particular party. But, Your Honours, in my submission, of course, a margin of deference must be given to an experienced counsel in this courtroom. Otherwise, of course, we will run into very considerable difficulties. And this is a matter that applies in the present instance to Ms. Nozica and the Stojic team, but it is a matter that will vex, no doubt, other Defence teams in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to consult on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After discussing the matter, the Trial Chamber grants you an hour for redirect, to be deducted from your overall time. Yes, Mr. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In view of your observation, noted on page 94, lines 17 and 18, I wish to make clear that the Defence for General Petkovic did not make the request for disqualification of any Judge, nor did it intend to do that. We were in a dilemma regarding a sentence spoken. And in accordance with our view that it is much better to openly ask a question about it than to comment about it in the corridors, I asked for an explanation of that sentence, and I am quite satisfied that it was a hypothetical situation. And we will be glad to continue these proceedings with the Trial Chamber as it stands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Well, 15 minutes for Mr. Bos to finish, then one hour for Ms. Nozica. Then the witness will be allowed to go back home. Thereafter, we shall resume, and Mr. Stringer filed a submission wanting to ask to intervene because there's still this pending issue of summaries. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We can raise this, Your Honour, tomorrow, Your Honour, but in fact we received additional information regarding the next witness over the weekend, and it's my understanding -- I will not be examining the next witness, but it's my understanding that the Prosecution is satisfied with the additional information that was provided to us over the weekend, after we sent yet another letter, but that we are going to be very, very attentive to the scope of the direct examination to make sure that it does not exceed the numerous summaries that have been provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I will address this issue tomorrow, with your leave. I do take objection to the Prosecution's conduct of itself in relation to this matter. They have issued and bandied about letters. It seems now they are complaining about the number of supplements, and so it appears now we're being blamed or criticised for the number of supplements and in a very sincere attempt to assist the opposing party. But, Your Honour, in my submission, and I will raise this tomorrow, the conduct of the Prosecution has been lamentable in this matter, and I will ask for ten minutes tomorrow to address this issue, because we can't have so much time wasted on every single witness so that the Defence is being ambushed or torpedoed to prepare summaries, when the Prosecution have failed to object since March 'til January for more detailed statements. They have not done that. Your Honours, I will address this tomorrow, hopefully with Mr. Scott in attendance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So once the witness -- this witness has left the courtroom, we shall resume, and you will be given ten minutes, Mr. Khan, to convey your observations. Thereafter, we'll have the witness brought in. So everybody is clear about everything. Very well. Witness, unfortunately, sir, you will have to stay here overnight. The Judges might be blamed, in part, because they put too many questions, but even so now Ms. Nozica wants another hour, so that it would have been impossible for you to leave today. So very much to our regret, you will have to stay. I hope this will not have a major repercussion on your family or professional life. And should it be so, do know that we regret it, but we couldn't do it any other way. I wish you all a very good evening. As you know, we shall work in the afternoon tomorrow, starting at 2.15. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
